text:
sara: Quick heads-up — ran calibration sweep comparing per-channel vs per-tensor INT8 for the fp8->int8 path on the 13B model. Strange mix: per-channel gives slightly better eval (avg ppl -0.8) but throughput dropped ~6% on our main CUDA kernel. Logs below.
kevin: numbers? and what was the calibration dataset composition?
sara: Throughput (tokens/s): baseline fp8 kernel = 1200, per-tensor INT8 = 1140, per-channel INT8 = 1070. Eval ppl on dev set: fp8=18.7, per-tensor=19.1, per-channel=18.3. Calibration set = 8k samples (3k code-ish, 3k docs+qa, 2k dialog). No percentile clipping used — pure min/max per-channel or per-tensor.
lena: 6% perf hit is non-trivial. Per-channel usually adds extra scale math and can change kernel selection. Did the runtime switch to a different GEMM kernel because of per-channel layout/strides?
rohan: sounds like kernel selection atm is based on quant params and strides. If per-channel quant changes memory access patterns, the dispatcher may pick a fallback kernel.
sara: exactly. Perf trace shows fallback to gemm_qk_custom_v2 instead of fused_qg_batched for that shape range. Also noticed higher L2 churn.
kevin: could outliers be blowing up ranges and causing different quant scales? If min/max has big outliers per-channel, scale^(-1) gets tiny and we overflow more, maybe fallback with saturation checks.
rohan: we should try percentile clipping (e.g., 99.5th) per-channel to ignore outliers. That often improves stability and avoids extreme scales.
lena: agree, but percentile clipping changes accuracy tradeoffs. We should test two things: 1) per-channel + 99.5 percentile clipping, 2) per-tensor + outlier removal (drop top 0.5% samples) and compare cost+accuracy+kernel choice.
sara: I'll run 1 and 2. Also noticed KV cache warmup behavior: quantized keys for per-channel had larger numeric dispersion early in generation causing more cache misses in our warmup heuristics (we evict earlier). Might explain latency tail.
kevin: interesting — can you paste the snippet of how you compute the clipping thresholds? small example helps.
sara: here's what I used locally:
```
# pseudo
vals = activations.reshape(-1)
lo, hi = np.percentile(vals, [0.5, 99.5])
scale = (hi - lo) / q_range
quantized = np.clip((vals - lo) / scale, qmin, qmax).astype(np.int8)
```
rohan: for per-channel you need to compute percentiles per out_channel dimension — do that on a subset to keep memory low. Also seed sampling to include long-code prompts so we catch tail behavior.
lena: sampling composition matters a lot. Your 3k code samples might be too uniform; propose stratified set: short dialog, long docs, code-with-long-strings, and adversarial prompts (extreme punctuation / long numeric tokens). These adversarial ones often create huge activation spikes.
sara: good call. I’ll expand the calibration set with ~200 adversarial examples and try 99.9 percentile as a sensitivity sweep.
kevin: also add a run with per-tensor but per-layer learnable scale (fake quant) to see effect on kernel path — if runtime still chooses fused kernel it's worth favoring per-tensor for perf.
rohan: misc note: profiling shows the kernel selection decision uses both quant metadata and sequence length distribution heuristics. We should log the decision reasons to perf traces so we can audit why a fallback was selected.
ci-bot: perf/job/4762 finished — artifacts: s3://redwood-perf/4762/logs, dashboard https://perf.redwood/4762
lena: awesome, attach those logs to the ticket. After runs, let's reconvene and pick the calibration default (likely per-tensor + percentile clipping or a hybrid scheme).
kevin: if per-channel keeps winning quality but loses throughput, maybe we make per-channel opt-in for customers who need quality; default to per-tensor+clipping.
sara: running jobs now (per-channel 99.5, per-channel 99.9, per-tensor + outlier-drop). will post summary in this thread when done. :hourglass:
rohan: thanks — please include kernel selection trace and KV cache eviction stats. small tables are fine.
sara: will do.
